# v1.1.0-dev.74 — Move your monitors, and every dialog is a window

Pre-release off the `dev` branch. Builds on `v1.1.0-dev.72`.

Two features, because dev.73 was never published — everything it
carried is in this build too.

## Rearrange Your Monitors

The Display editor already drew your monitors to scale, sitting where
they actually sit. Now you can move them, and a profile can remember
where you put them.

Grab a monitor in the picker and drag it. It behaves the way the same
boxes behave in Windows' own Display Settings: it clicks onto a
neighbour's edge when it comes close, gets pushed back out if you drop
it on top of something, and gets pulled back into contact if you drop
it out in space. A short drag still selects, so picking a display to
change its resolution works exactly as before.

No mouse: select a display, then hold **Shift** and press an arrow
key. That moves it to that side of its nearest neighbour — not by some
number of pixels, but flush against it. Press the same key twice and
the second press changes nothing, which is the point.

### Three Rules Windows Enforces Quietly

Windows will accept an arrangement it doesn't like and then rewrite
it, which is how you end up with monitors somewhere you never put
them. WLM settles the layout first instead:

- The primary monitor sits at the origin. Move the primary and
  everything else is re-expressed around it.
- Nothing overlaps. Drop one monitor on another and the one under your
  hand is the one that gives way.
- Nothing floats. Every display has to touch another one, so a gap
  gets closed rather than left for Windows to close its own way.

Sometimes settling a layout means moving a monitor you weren't
touching — a saved arrangement reapplied after one of those displays
changed resolution no longer fits itself, and something has to give.
It says which monitor it had to move rather than letting you find out
by looking.

Getting that right took measuring rather than reasoning. The first
version treated "don't move this one" as absolute, which sounds
correct and isn't: pull the middle monitor out of a row of three and
the two either side stop touching, so a rule that can't move either of
them has to give up. Across a 5,643-drop sweep it gave up on 2,856 —
half of them. Now it's zero, across 22,035.

That sweep also caught a deadlock worth naming. Drop a tall monitor
into the crack between two short ones and the old repair pushed it off
the left neighbour onto the right, off the right one back onto the
left, forever. Now a move has to clear the whole desk before it's
allowed, so the monitor pops out above the pair instead of bouncing
between them.

### Saving It

Save the profile and the arrangement goes with it, alongside the
scaling and resolution that were already there. Loading the profile
puts the monitors back before your windows are restored.

Positions are saved for **every** monitor, not only the ones that
moved. An arrangement is a fact about the whole desk — "the portrait
one is on the left" means nothing without knowing where the other one
is — so saving half of it would restore a different layout on any day
the rest had drifted.

Order matters and is fixed: resolution and orientation first, then the
arrangement. Changing a resolution changes the size of the very
rectangle being placed. The arrangement then goes in as one atomic
commit rather than one monitor at a time, because moving them one by
one walks through overlapping layouts that Windows repairs on the
spot.

A profile can carry an arrangement and nothing else. Tick
**Display-only preset** and it becomes a hotkey that rearranges your
desk.

The 15-second Keep-or-Revert bar after **Apply now** now snapshots
where your monitors were, not just their resolutions. Rearranging is
the one change here that survives a reboot, so it's the one that most
needed an undo that works when you can't read the screen.

## Every Dialog Is Its Own Window

Dialogs used to be panels drawn over the app. Each one is now a real
window: drag it onto another monitor, resize it, put it where you
want it.

It opens at the app window's size less 50px, centred on it. After that
it's yours, and nothing springs back to full size the next time you
open it.

The app is disabled while a dialog is up, and that's the operating
system doing it rather than a panel sitting on top — keystrokes can't
reach the window behind. It's blurred so it reads as out of play, and
clicking it points you back at the dialog.

Open a dialog from inside a dialog — the resolution list from the
display editor, a confirm over anything — and it stacks in the window
you're already looking at rather than spawning a third one somewhere
else for you to hunt down.

Two things deliberately stayed as panels. The command palette is built
on the same chrome but it's a quick-open list, not a dialog. The help
overlay is a toggle over the app rather than something you answer.

## The Window Editor's Missing Padding

The edit-window dialog had a comfortable margin down its left side and
essentially none on its right. That turned out to be arithmetic rather
than taste.

Its form is a two-column grid, and a column set to `1fr` will still
refuse to be narrower than its widest content — for a dropdown, its
longest option. "Desktop 2 (saved-current)" pushed the left column
21px past its share, and the whole grid slid right by that much.
Measured before: 22px of gap on the left, 1.2px on the right. Both
sides match now, and the columns can no longer push past the edge no
matter what goes in them.

## Under The Hood

A dialog window loads the same page the app does, with a flag that
says "show only this dialog". No dialog's markup or behaviour moved
anywhere, which is why sixteen of them could change at once without
each becoming its own rewrite.

The one exception is the window editor, because it's the only dialog
with live state behind it — undo history, the unsaved-changes flag,
the view redrawing as you type. Reading the profile from disk in the
dialog would have quietly dropped any unsaved edit, so it stays a
remote control: you type in the dialog, the app window applies it, and
there's still exactly one undo history.

The screenshot tour that generates the website's images follows
dialogs into their new windows. Without that it would have kept
capturing the blurred app window sitting behind them, which is the
kind of drift that isn't noticed until it ships.

## Install

Auto-updates from dev.53 and later. Otherwise unzip and run.
